RagShortTexts: William of Saliceto's surgical text of 1275 is not a completed book in 1259.
Period wound-care practices do not prove modern antisepsis or guaranteed survival.

Variants.Content: William of Saliceto is an active physician and teacher in northern Italy in the mid-thirteenth century, but his best-known surgical work has not yet been completed in 1259. He belongs to a learned medical culture in which physicians debate how to treat wounds, when to drain an abscess and how much trust to place in inherited Galenic teaching. A practitioner may favour careful incision, ligature or wine cleansing based on experience, while another relies more heavily on cautery. These are competing practices rather than a settled revolution led by a published textbook. The treatise later called Chirurgia is still ahead, so contemporaries cannot quote its finished arguments or know its later reputation.

William of Saliceto's later surgical writing belongs to a developing learned tradition, not a completed textbook available in 1259. A contemporary healer may discuss training and wound care without predicting the contents of a work dated 1275. Wine dressings and ligatures are period practices to describe critically, rather than proof of modern antisepsis or guaranteed survival.
